_comment: Guided tour for the filtered-FCS filter calculator. This tool is a plain QWidget wired through attach_help_and_guide, so targets are toolbar actions and dock tab titles. It ships a built-in example decay, so the tour can be walked with no data of the user's own. Read by chisurf.gui.widgets.tools.guided_tour.

steps.title: What filtering buys you
steps.text:
Plain FCS correlates the total intensity. Two species with the same diffusion time cannot be separated by it — there is nothing in one intensity trace to separate.

But every photon also carries a nanosecond arrival time after the excitation pulse, and different species decay differently. This tool turns those decay patterns into per-photon weights, and correlating the weighted streams gives species-selective curves. Seven steps, on the built-in example.

steps.title: The mixed decay you are separating
steps.text:
The tool opens with an example already loaded, so you can walk this whole tour without a file of your own.

For real work this is where a measured mixed decay goes — the histogram containing every species at once. Everything else on this page is about explaining this curve as a sum of components.

steps.title: Where the component patterns come from
steps.text:
Auto-fit decomposes the mixed decay into N lifetime components and offers them as species.

Treat it as a starting set, not an answer: fitting two components to a three-component sample gives you two patterns that are each a blend of the truth, and nothing in the fit will say so.

Measured references — the pure species, run separately under the same optics — are better whenever you can get them.

await.hint: Press 🎯 Auto-fit to decompose the example decay.

steps.title: The limit you cannot buy your way out of
steps.text:
Two lifetimes within roughly 20 % of each other cannot be separated, no matter how many photons you collect.

What happens instead is worse than failure: the filter amplitudes blow up and the "separated" curves are amplified noise that looks perfectly clean. Watch the component list — if the fitted lifetimes crowd together, stop and reconsider the model rather than adding photons.

steps.title: Compute the filters
steps.text: Unmix fits non-negative component intensities and computes the filter for each species.

steps.title: Filters go negative, and that is correct
steps.text:
A filter value is not a probability. Negative weights are how the method subtracts a component's expected contribution from the part of the decay it shares with another — that subtraction is the separation.

The number to watch is the magnitude. Values in the tens or hundreds mean an ill-conditioned separation, not a sensitive one. And a filter set that never goes negative usually means the patterns were never distinguishable in the first place.

steps.title: Three checks, and one thing not to forget
steps.text:
1. Does the reconstruction match the measured decay? If the components cannot rebuild it, they do not describe the sample.
2. Are the species cross-correlations flat for species that do not interconvert? Structure there is the most direct evidence the patterns are wrong.
3. Change the number of components. A real separation is stable; an over-specified one redistributes wildly.

And: scatter is a component too. Scattered excitation has its own pattern — essentially the IRF — and if you do not give it one, it is absorbed into the others and distorts them both.

The ? button has the long version.
